work: Enarratio in Epistolam B. Pauli ad Hebræos
source: Dionysii Cartusiani Opera Omnia, t. XIII (Montreuil)

1.title: EXPOSITIO CAPITULI PRIMI : MULTIFARIE MULTISQUE MODIS, ETC.
1.title_en: Exposition of the first chapter: God, who, at sundry times and in divers manners, etc.

paras.t: Postquam ergo Apostolus Ecclesiam Latinorum, puta Romanos, Ecclesiam quoque Græcorum, videlicet Corinthios, Galatas, Thessalonicenses, etc., scripto edocuit, novissime Ecclesiam Hebræorum per epistolam instruit; ostendensque Christi excellentiam, et novi Testamenti præ veteri dignitatem, ita exorsus est :
paras.en: After the Apostle, then, had taught in writing the Church of the Latins, that is, the Romans, and the Church of the Greeks also, namely the Corinthians, Galatians, Thessalonians, etc., last of all he instructs the Church of the Hebrews by an epistle; and, showing the excellence of Christ and the dignity of the New Testament above the Old, he began thus:

paras.t: Multifarie, id est frequenter repetitisque vicibus, seu diversis sermonibus, figurativis, obscuris et mysticis, multisque modis, id est distinctis visionum generibus seu variis modis loquendi, videlicet : interdum per visionem imaginariam, quemadmodum Isaias vidit Dominum sedentem super solium excelsum, et Jeremias vidit ollam succensam et virgam vigilantem ; interdum per visionem exteriorem, sicut Daniel vidit Gabrielem, et Jacob angelum secum luctantem; interdum per inspirationem anagogicam seu pure intellectualem, ut in David; quandoque in somno, quandoque in vigilia; olim, id est præteritis diuque elapsis temporibus, Deus loquens patribus, id est præcessoribus nostris, Patriarchis, et ceteris bonis hominibus : de quibus ait Virgo benedicta, Sicut locutus est ad patres nostros, Abraham et semini ejus; in Prophetis, id est per Prophetas, quibus per angelos loquebatur. Sed et inferioribus angelis loquitur per superiores. Unde apud Lucam habetur : Sicut locutus est per os sanctorum, qui a sæculo sunt, Prophetarum ejus. Hinc quoque per Prophetam Dominus loquitur : Ego visiones multiplicavi, et in manibus Prophetarum assimilatus sum.
paras.en: [[1:1|At sundry times|Multifarie]], that is, frequently and at repeated times, or in divers discourses, figurative, obscure and mystical; [[1:1|and in divers manners|multisque modis]], that is, by distinct kinds of visions or various manners of speaking, namely: sometimes by an imaginary vision [that is, one seen in the imagination, not with the bodily eyes], as Isaias [[Is 6:1|saw the Lord sitting upon a throne high|vidit Dominum sedentem super solium excelsum]], and Jeremias saw [[Jer 1:13|a boiling caldron|ollam succensam]] and [[Jer 1:11|a rod watching|virgam vigilantem]]; sometimes by an exterior vision, as Daniel saw Gabriel[[Dan 8:16||]][[Dan 9:21||]], and Jacob the angel wrestling with him[[Gen 32:25||]]; sometimes by an anagogical or purely intellectual inspiration, as in David[[2 Kings 23:2||]]; at times in sleep, at times awake; [[1:1|in times past|olim]], that is, in times gone by and long since elapsed, [[1:1|God|Deus]] [[1:1|spoke|loquens]] [[1:1|to the fathers|patribus]], that is, to our forerunners, the Patriarchs and the other good men: of whom the blessed Virgin says, [[Luke 1:55|As he spoke to our fathers: to Abraham and to his seed|Sicut locutus est ad patres nostros, Abraham et semini ejus]]; [[1:1|by the prophets|in Prophetis]], that is, through the Prophets, to whom he spoke through angels. And he speaks to the lower angels too through the higher. Hence it is said in Luke: [[Luke 1:70|As he spoke by the mouth of his holy prophets, who are from the beginning|Sicut locutus est per os sanctorum, qui a sæculo sunt, Prophetarum ejus]]. Hence also the Lord speaks by the Prophet: [[Osee 12:10|I have multiplied visions, and I have used similitudes by the ministry of the prophets|Ego visiones multiplicavi, et in manibus Prophetarum assimilatus sum]].

paras.t: Novissime, id est in hac ultima mundi ætate (de qua dicit Joannes, Carissimi, novissima hora est) : nos enim sumus in quos fines sæculorum devenerunt : diebus istis, id est tempore gratiæ. Unde scriptum est : Erit in novissimis diebus præparatus mons domus Domini. Locutus est nobis in Filio, id est per Unigenitum suum incarnatum, qui in Evangelio asserit : Mea doctrina non est mea, sed ejus qui misit me; rursusque : Verba quæ ego loquor, a me ipso non loquor. Quem constituit Deus Pater heredem universorum, id est possessorem ac Dominum omnium rerum creatarum, loquendo de Christo secundum naturam assumptam : sic enim constitutus est omnium Dominus. Nam ea […] ipso, quo Christi humanitas a Verbo assumpta est ad esse increatum, convenit ei, toti creaturæ præferri ac dominari. Propter quod ipse ait : Data est mihi omnis potestas in cœlo et in terra; et iterum, Pater diligit Filium, et omnia dedit in manu ejus. Hoc et in Psalmo cantatur : Postula a me, et dabo tibi gentes hereditatem tuam.
paras.en: [[1:1|last of all|Novissime]] [in the Vulgate this word begins verse 2], that is, in this last age of the world (of which John says, Dearly beloved, [[1 John 2:18|it is the last hour|novissima hora est]]): for we are they [[1 Cor 10:11|upon whom the ends of the world are come|in quos fines sæculorum devenerunt]]: [[1:2|In these days|diebus istis]], that is, in the time of grace. Hence it is written: [[Is 2:2|in the last days the mountain of the house of the Lord shall be prepared|Erit in novissimis diebus præparatus mons domus Domini]]. [[1:2|Hath spoken to us by his Son|Locutus est nobis in Filio]], that is, through his only-begotten Son incarnate, who declares in the Gospel: [[John 7:16|My doctrine is not mine, but his that sent me|Mea doctrina non est mea, sed ejus qui misit me]]; and again: [[John 14:10|The words that I speak to you, I speak not of myself|Verba quæ ego loquor, a me ipso non loquor]]. [[1:2|Whom he hath appointed|Quem constituit]] God the Father [[1:2|heir of all things|heredem universorum]], that is, the possessor and Lord of all created things, speaking of Christ according to the nature he assumed: for so was he appointed Lord of all things[[1 Cor 15:27||]]. For […][[Ps 8:7||]] [the margin gives Ps. viii, 7 beside this damaged line; the words there are lost] by the very fact that the humanity of Christ was assumed by the Word to uncreated being [that is, into the personal being of the uncreated Word], it belongs to it to be set above all creation and to rule over it. For which reason he himself says: [[Matt 28:18|All power is given to me in heaven and in earth|Data est mihi omnis potestas in cœlo et in terra]]; and again, [[John 3:35|The Father loveth the Son: and he hath given all things into his hand|Pater diligit Filium, et omnia dedit in manu ejus]]. This is sung in the Psalm also: [[Ps 2:8|Ask of me, and I will give thee the Gentiles for thy inheritance|Postula a me, et dabo tibi gentes hereditatem tuam]].

paras.t: Per quem fecit et sæcula, id est temporalia omnia. Omnia enim per ipsum facta sunt, et sine ipso factum est nihil. Hoc convenit Christo secundum divinam naturam. Non enim per Filium facta sunt quasi per ministrum vel instrumentum, sed sicut per principalem agentem, qui cum Patre idem est factor, quemadmodum ipse affirmat : Quæcumque facit Pater, hæc et Filius similiter facit. Hoc tamen quod dicitur, Per ipsum, proprie spectat ad Filium, cui convenit causalitas causæ exemplaris, quum sit exemplar omnium rerum et ars rationibus plena.
paras.en: [[1:2|By whom also he made the world|Per quem fecit et sæcula]] [*sæcula*, literally "the ages"], that is, all temporal things. For [[John 1:3|All things were made by him: and without him was made nothing|Omnia enim per ipsum facta sunt, et sine ipso factum est nihil]]. This belongs to Christ according to his divine nature. For things were not made by the Son as by a servant or an instrument, but as by the principal agent, who is one and the same maker with the Father, as he himself affirms: [[John 5:19|what things soever he doth, these the Son also doth in like manner|Quæcumque facit Pater, hæc et Filius similiter facit]]. Yet the words *by him* belong properly to the Son, to whom belongs the causality of the exemplar cause, since he is the exemplar of all things and the art full of reasons [*rationes*: the divine ideas, the patterns after which all things are made].

paras.t: Qui quum sit splendor gloriæ, id est radius sapientiæ Patris ingenitæ, seu candor lucis æternæ, et fulgor majestatis paternæ, in quo plene resplendet tota perfectio Patris. Est namque Filius, mentis paternæ verbum æternum, intelligibilis dictio, et sapientiæ ejus plena expressio. Dicitur ergo Filius splendor gloriæ seu excellentiæ Dei Patris, quoniam quidquid Patris est, splendet ac lucet in Filio. Et in hoc insinuatur coæternitas Filii cum Patre. Splendor enim est igni seu soli coævus : et si sol ab æterno fuisset, splendor fuisset ei consempiternus.
paras.en: [[1:3|Who being the brightness of his glory|Qui quum sit splendor gloriæ]], that is, the ray of the unbegotten wisdom of the Father, or [[Wis 7:26|the brightness of eternal light|candor lucis æternæ]], and the splendour of the Father's majesty, in whom the whole perfection of the Father shines forth in its fulness. For the Son is the eternal word of the Father's mind, his intelligible utterance, and the full expression of his wisdom. The Son, then, is called the brightness of the glory, or excellence, of God the Father, because whatever is the Father's shines and is bright in the Son[[John 10:30||]][[John 16:15||]]. And in this the coeternity of the Son with the Father is suggested. For brightness is coeval with the fire or the sun: and if the sun had been from eternity, its brightness would have been coeternal with it.

paras.t: Et figura, id est imago vel character (in Græco quippe habetur, χαρακτήρ), substantiæ ejus, id est ipsius Patris, qui est substantia seu divina essentia. Græci vero utuntur nomine substantiæ indifferenter pro essentia et persona. Dicit autem Apostolus, Figura, quamvis figura proprie locum non habeat nisi in corporalibus rebus. Per figuram enim res maxime cognoscitur, et in ea similitudo attenditur unius cum alio. Quoniam ergo Filius Patri per omnia similis, imo simillimus est, non distinctus ab eo, nisi quia ab eo, et Patrem repræsentat, eumque notificavit in tantum ut ipse dixerit, Qui videt me, videt et Patrem; idcirco Filius appellatur figura substantiæ Patris : in quo designatur consubstantialitas Patris et Filii. Filius equidem est imago naturalis et essentialis, non imitativa et artificialis, Dei Patris, quemadmodum filius regis est imago patris regnantis. In tali autem imagine invenitur natura ejus cujus est imago. Quum ergo divina essentia sit simplex ac indivisibilis, constat quod eadem numero sit in Patre ac Filio. Propter quod ait : Ego et Pater unum sumus; et, Quæcumque habet Pater, mea sunt.
paras.en: [[1:3|And the figure|Et figura]], that is, the image or character (for in the Greek it is χαρακτήρ), [[1:3|of his substance|substantiæ ejus]], that is, of the Father himself, who is substance, or the divine essence. The Greeks, however, use the word *substance* indifferently for essence and for person. Now the Apostle says *figure*, although figure properly has place only in bodily things. For by its figure a thing is chiefly known, and in it the likeness of one thing to another is observed. Since, then, the Son is like the Father in all things, nay, most like him, not distinct from him except in being from him, and represents the Father, and has made him known, so far that he himself said, [[John 14:9|he that seeth me seeth the Father also|Qui videt me, videt et Patrem]]; therefore the Son is called the figure of the Father's substance: and in this the consubstantiality of the Father and the Son is signified. For the Son is the natural and essential image of God the Father, not an imitative and artificial one, as the son of a king is the image of the reigning father. And in such an image is found the nature of him whose image it is. Since, then, the divine essence is simple and indivisible, it is certain that it is numerically the same in the Father and in the Son. For which reason he says: [[John 10:30|I and the Father are one|Ego et Pater unum sumus]]; and, [[John 16:15|All things whatsoever the Father hath are mine|Quæcumque habet Pater, mea sunt]].

paras.t: Portansque Filius, id est sustentans, conservans et moderans, omnia creata, visibilia et invisibilia, verbo virtutis suæ, id est suæ potestatis imperio seu influxu. Quemadmodum enim omnia per ipsum facta sunt, sic sine ejus continua conservatione redigerentur in nihilum : quia plus dependet creatura a Creatore, quam radius a sole. In hoc autem notatur æqualitas Filii cum Patre in potestate, quæ etiam una et eadem est in tribus Personis.
paras.en: [[1:3|And upholding|Portansque]], the Son, that is, sustaining, preserving and governing, [[1:3|all things|omnia]] created, visible and invisible, [[1:3|by the word of his power|verbo virtutis suæ]], that is, by the command or influence of his might. For as [[John 1:3|all things were made by him|omnia per ipsum facta sunt]], so without his continual preservation they would be brought back to nothing: for the creature depends more on the Creator than the ray on the sun. And in this the equality of the Son with the Father in power is noted, which power is also one and the same in the three Persons.

paras.t: Denique, his quæ dicta sunt de similitudine Filii cum Patre, consonat quod de increata et ingenita Sapientia scribitur in libro Sapientiæ : Vapor est virtutis Dei, et emanatio quædam claritatis omnipotentis Dei sincera; candor est enim lucis æternæ, et speculum sine macula Dei majestatis, et imago bonitatis illius. De sempiternitate vero Filius ait per Sapientem : Ego ex ore Altissimi prodivi, primogenita ante omnem creaturam.
paras.en: Lastly, with what has been said of the likeness of the Son to the Father there agrees what is written of the uncreated and unbegotten Wisdom in the book of Wisdom: She is [[Wis 7:25|a vapour of the power of God, and a certain pure emmanation of the glory of the Almighty God|Vapor est virtutis Dei, et emanatio quædam claritatis omnipotentis Dei sincera]]; [[Wis 7:26|For she is the brightness of eternal light, and the unspotted mirror of God's majesty, and the image of his goodness|candor est enim lucis æternæ, et speculum sine macula Dei majestatis, et imago bonitatis illius]]. And of his everlastingness the Son says by the Wise Man: [[Ecclus 24:5|I came out of the mouth of the most High, the firstborn before all creatures|Ego ex ore Altissimi prodivi, primogenita ante omnem creaturam]].

paras.t: Sed objici potest : Quum Filius sit Verbum Patris, si Filius omnia portat verbo virtutis suæ, ergo Verbi est Verbum. Et respondendum, quod Verbum in tali locutione æquivoce sumitur. Verbi autem non est Verbum, sumendo Verbum univoce. Quum vero dicitur, Portans omnia verbo virtutis suæ, accipitur verbum pro imperio, sicut in Psalmo, ubi dicitur : Ignis, grando, nix, glacies, spiritus procellarum, quæ faciunt verbum ejus : et alibi : Emittet verbum suum, et liquefaciet ea.
paras.en: But it may be objected: since the Son is the Word of the Father, if the Son upholds all things by the word of his power, then there is a Word of the Word. And the answer is that *word* in such a phrase is taken equivocally [that is, in a different sense]. But there is no Word of the Word, taking *Word* univocally [that is, in one and the same sense]. When it is said, [[1:3|upholding all things by the word of his power|Portans omnia verbo virtutis suæ]], *word* is taken for command, as in the Psalm, where it is said: [[Ps 148:8|Fire, hail, snow, ice, stormy winds, which fulfil his word|Ignis, grando, nix, glacies, spiritus procellarum, quæ faciunt verbum ejus]] [the margin gives Ps. cxviii, 8; the verse is Ps 148:8]; and elsewhere: [[Ps 147:7|He shall send out his word, and shall melt them|Emittet verbum suum, et liquefaciet ea]] [the margin gives Ps. cxlvii, 18, as the verse is numbered in the Hebrew; in the Vulgate it is Ps 147:7].

paras.t: Purgationem peccatorum faciens, id est peccatores emundans, seu peccata originalia et actualia merito suæ sanctissimæ passionis delens, juxta illud propheticum: Ipse autem vulneratus est propter iniquitates nostras, attritus est propter scelera nostra. Et Joannes ait : Ecce Agnus Dei qui tollit peccata mundi. Sedet in throno gloriæ, id est, tanquam omnium judex ac Dominus quiescit et residet, ad dexteram majestatis, id est ad æqualitatem summi et gloriosi Dei Patris, secundum suam deitatem. Sic enim æqualis est Patri : imo Patris et Filii est una majestas ac dignitas. Si vero referatur ad Christum secundum assumptam humanitatem, tunc dicitur sedere ad dexteram majestatis paternæ, id est in potioribus bonis Dei Patris, quibus et copiosissime fruitur. In excelsis, id est in cœlestibus, scilicet in cœlo empyreo, loco et dignitate omnibus altior. Unde ipse ait : Ego vici, et sedi cum Patre meo in throno ejus. Hæc autem sessio Christi non opponitur stationi. Ideo interdum dicitur stare, prout Stephanus dicebat : Video cœlos apertos, et Filium hominis stantem a dextris virtutis Dei; et Isaias, Stat ad judicandum Dominus. Stat enim, quasi paratus ad operandum: sedet vero, tanquam stabiliter permanens ubi est.
paras.en: [[1:3|Making purgation of sins|Purgationem peccatorum faciens]], that is, cleansing sinners, or blotting out original and actual sins by the merit of his most holy passion, according to that saying of the Prophet: [[Is 53:5|But he was wounded for our iniquities, he was bruised for our sins|Ipse autem vulneratus est propter iniquitates nostras, attritus est propter scelera nostra]]. And John says: [[John 1:29|Behold the Lamb of God. Behold him who taketh away the sin of the world|Ecce Agnus Dei qui tollit peccata mundi]]. He [[1:3|sitteth|Sedet]] on the throne of glory, that is, he rests and abides as the judge and Lord of all[[Acts 10:42||]], [[1:3|on the right hand of the majesty|ad dexteram majestatis]], that is, in equality with the most high and glorious God the Father, according to his Godhead. For so he is equal to the Father: nay, the Father and the Son have one majesty and dignity. But if it is referred to Christ according to the humanity he assumed, then he is said to sit at the right hand of the Father's majesty, that is, in the greater goods of God the Father, which he also enjoys most abundantly. [[1:3|On high|In excelsis]], that is, in the heavenly places, namely in the empyrean heaven [that is, the highest heaven, the dwelling of the blessed], higher than all in place and in dignity. Hence he himself says: [[Apoc 3:21|I also have overcome and am set down with my Father in his throne|Ego vici, et sedi cum Patre meo in throno ejus]]. Now this sitting of Christ is not opposed to standing. Therefore he is sometimes said to stand, as Stephen said: [[Acts 7:55|I see the heavens opened and the Son of man standing on the right hand of God|Video cœlos apertos, et Filium hominis stantem a dextris virtutis Dei]] [Denis reads "on the right hand of the power of God"]; and Isaias: [[Is 3:13|The Lord standeth up to judge|Stat ad judicandum Dominus]]. For he stands as one ready to act; but he sits as one abiding steadfastly where he is.

paras.t: Tanto melior, id est per gratiam unionis et habitualem dignior, angelis effectus secundum humanam naturam, secundum quam accepit gratiam Spiritus Sancti non ad mensuram : angeli vero ad mensuram sortiti sunt eam ; quanto differentius, id est sublimiori modo; vel, Differentius, id est excellentius, præ illis nomen hereditavit, id est, jure æterno a Patre accepit, firmiterque possedit. De quo nomine Philippensibus dictum est supra : Deus exaltavit illum, et dedit illi nomen quod est super omne nomen, videlicet, ut ille homo vocetur verus Deus, atque unigenitus Dei Filius, non per adoptionem, sed per naturam, quemadmodum ait Scriptura : Simus in vero Filio ejus Jesu Christo: hic est verus Deus et vita æterna. Tale autem nomen non competit angelis. Verumtamen in Psalmo dicitur Christus paulo minus minoratus ab angelis. Sed hoc intelligitur de Christo quantum ad assumptæ naturæ passibilitatem et mortem ac sepulturam. In resurrectione vero ac ascensione præ angelis glorificatus est, etiam in humana natura. Sciendum vero, quod Christus in quantum homo, a primo instanti suæ conceptionis in Virgine, absolute loquendo, prælatus est angelis, et omnium creaturarum Dominus constitutus, propter personalem cum Verbo unionem et gratiæ plenitudinem singularem. Sed ista prælatio post resurrectionem manifestata est. Unde et Christus dixit : Pater, clarifica Filium tuum. Porro humanitas Christi, quum sit ejusdem speciei cum aliis, non est melior natura angelica, secundum sua essentialia; sed per dona gratiæ melior ea effecta est. Hanc excellentiam Christi consequenter probat Apostolus.
paras.en: [[1:4|Being made so much better|Tanto melior]], that is, more worthy through the grace of union and habitual grace [the grace of union is the joining of his manhood to the Person of the Word; habitual grace, the grace abiding in his soul], [[1:4|than the angels|angelis effectus]], according to his human nature, according to which he received the grace of the Holy Ghost not by measure[[John 3:34||]], whereas the angels received it by measure; [[1:4|as he hath inherited a more excellent|quanto differentius]], that is, in a more sublime manner; or, *more excellent* [literally "more differently"], that is, more excellently, [[1:4|name than they|præ illis nomen hereditavit]], that is, he received it from the Father by eternal right, and held it firmly. Of which name it is said above, to the Philippians: [[Phil 2:9|God also hath exalted him and hath given him a name which is above all names|Deus exaltavit illum, et dedit illi nomen quod est super omne nomen]], namely, that that man should be called true God and the only-begotten Son of God, not by adoption but by nature, as the Scripture says: [[1 John 5:20|may be in his true Son|Simus in vero Filio ejus]] Jesus Christ: [[1 John 5:20|This is the true God and life eternal|hic est verus Deus et vita æterna]]. But such a name does not belong to the angels. Yet in the Psalm Christ is said to be made a little lower than the angels[[Ps 8:6||]]. But this is understood of Christ as to the passibility of the nature he assumed, and his death and burial. In his resurrection and ascension, however, he was glorified above the angels, even in his human nature. But it must be known that Christ as man, from the first instant of his conception in the Virgin, absolutely speaking, was set above the angels and appointed Lord of all creatures, because of his personal union with the Word and his singular fulness of grace. But this preeminence was made manifest after the resurrection. Hence Christ also said: Father, [[John 17:1|Glorify thy Son|clarifica Filium tuum]]. Further, the humanity of Christ, since it is of the same species as that of other men, is not better than the angelic nature in what belongs to its essence; but by the gifts of grace it has been made better than it. This excellence of Christ the Apostle next proves.

paras.t: Cui enim dixit Pater aliquando (ab exordio creationis) angelorum? quasi dicat. Nulli angelo unquam dixit Pater quod subditur : Filius meus es tu, ego hodie, id est in æternitate, in qua semper est hodie, id est instans invariabile, non habens præteritum vel futurum, genui te generatione vera ac intellectuali, id est, de mea substantia produxi te, communicando tibi essentiam meam. Hoc certum est dici non posse de aliquo angelo. Nam licet angeli appellentur filii Dei, non tamen sunt filii ejusdem naturæ cum Creatore; nec proprie geniti sunt, sed creati; non hodie, sed in exordio mundi. Dicit ergo Pater ad Filium, Genui, per modum præteriti, ne generatio ejus nova vel modo inchoata putetur. Dicit quoque, Hodie, ne præterita æstimetur. Ut ergo generatio Filii agnoscatur invariabilis et æterna, dicit, Hodie genui, copulando præsens præterito. In æternitate quippe nihil præteritum est, quasi desierit; nihil futurum, quasi nondum sit : sed quidquid æternum est, semper est. Hanc auctoritatem sumpsit Apostolus ex Psalmo, quem ad litteram scriptum esse de Christo frequenter testatur liber Actuum Apostolorum. Idcirco recentiores Judæorum doctores, qui psalmum illum ad litteram exponunt de David, plurimum errant, et ab antiquis Hebræorum doctoribus discrepant.
paras.en: [[1:5|For to which of the angels hath he said at any time|Cui enim dixit Pater aliquando (ab exordio creationis) angelorum]]? (He means the Father, and *at any time* from the beginning of creation.) As if to say: To no angel did the Father ever say what follows: [[1:5|Thou art my Son, to-day|Filius meus es tu, ego hodie]][[Ps 2:7||]], that is, in eternity, in which it is always to-day, that is, an unchanging instant, having no past or future, [[1:5|have I begotten thee|genui te]] by a true and intellectual generation, that is, I have brought thee forth from my substance, communicating to thee my essence. It is certain that this cannot be said of any angel. For although the angels are called sons of God, yet they are not sons of the same nature as the Creator; nor are they properly begotten, but created; not to-day, but in the beginning of the world. The Father, then, says to the Son, *I have begotten*, in the form of the past, lest his generation be thought new or only lately begun. He says also, *to-day*, lest it be reckoned past. So, that the generation of the Son may be acknowledged as unchanging and eternal, he says, *to-day have I begotten*, joining the present to the past. For in eternity nothing is past, as though it had ceased; nothing future, as though it were not yet: but whatever is eternal, always is. The Apostle took this authority from the Psalm, which the book of the Acts of the Apostles often testifies was written literally of Christ[[Acts 13:33||]]. Therefore the more recent doctors of the Jews, who expound that psalm literally of David, err greatly, and disagree with the ancient doctors of the Hebrews.

paras.t: Consequenter inducit Apostolus aliud testimonium ad idem probandum. Et rursus Deus Pater ait : Ego ero illi in patrem, id est, Pater Christi ero, quia æternaliter Pater ipsius sum. Æternitas autem omnem temporis differentiam comprehendit : ideo per quodlibet tempus designatur. Simili modo ait Salvator de Spiritu Sancto : Quæcumque audiet, loquetur; et, Ille me clarificabit, quia de meo accipiet. Si autem intelligatur dictum per modum præteriti, referendum est ad tempus incarnationis et manifestationis Christi. Nam qui æternaliter Pater Christi fuit, secundum quod Deus, futurus fuit Pater Christi hominis de Virgine tunc nascituri, jam nati : et hoc ipsum manifestatum est mundo post adventum Spiritus Sancti per prædicationem Apostolorum. Et ipse erit mihi in filium, id est, Filius meus erit atque vocabitur, prout prædixerat angelus : Hic erit magnus, et Filius Altissimi vocabitur. Unde Christo baptizato, et transfigurato, vox Patris audita est, dicens : Hic est Filius meus dilectus, in quo mihi complacui. Ideo Archiapostolus in secunda sua Canonica : Accepit (inquit) a Deo Patre honorem et gloriam, voce ad eum delapsa hujuscemodi a magnifica gloria : Hic est Filius meus, etc.
paras.en: Next the Apostle brings in another testimony to prove the same. [[1:5|And again|Et rursus]] God the Father says: [[1:5|I will be to him a Father|Ego ero illi in patrem]], that is, I will be the Father of Christ, because I am his Father eternally. Now eternity contains every difference of time: therefore it is signified by any tense. In like manner the Saviour says of the Holy Ghost: [[John 16:13|what things soever he shall hear, he shall speak|Quæcumque audiet, loquetur]]; and, [[John 16:14|He shall glorify me: because he shall receive of mine|Ille me clarificabit, quia de meo accipiet]]. But if it is understood as said in the manner of the past, it is to be referred to the time of the incarnation and manifestation of Christ. For he who was eternally the Father of Christ, according as he is God, was to be the Father of Christ the man, then to be born of the Virgin, now born: and this very thing was made manifest to the world after the coming of the Holy Ghost, by the preaching of the Apostles. [[1:5|And he shall be to me a Son|Et ipse erit mihi in filium]], that is, he shall be my Son and shall be called so, as the angel had foretold: [[Luke 1:32|He shall be great and shall be called the Son of the Most High|Hic erit magnus, et Filius Altissimi vocabitur]]. Hence when Christ was baptized, and when he was transfigured, the voice of the Father was heard, saying: [[Matt 3:17|This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased|Hic est Filius meus dilectus, in quo mihi complacui]] [so at the baptism; at the Transfiguration, Matt 17:5]. Therefore the Chief of the Apostles says in his second Canonical Epistle: [[2 Pet 1:17|he received|Accepit]] (he says) [[2 Pet 1:17|from God the Father honour and glory, this voice coming down to him from the excellent glory: This is my beloved Son|a Deo Patre honorem et gloriam, voce ad eum delapsa hujuscemodi a magnifica gloria : Hic est Filius meus]], etc.

paras.t: Secundum Glossam (et est glossa Chrysostomi), hoc testimonium Apostoli nunc allegatum, ex Isaia assumptum est : quod tamen nostra non habet translatio, quantum ad formam verborum. Sed quantum ad sensum, dicere possumus quod sumptum sit ex eo quod ibi habetur secundum allegationem Matthæi evangelistæ : Ecce puer meus electus quem elegi, etc. Probabilius vero apparet, quod sumptum sit ex secundo Regum et primo Paralipomenon, ubi hæc verba in propria forma continentur. Sed tunc dubitatio oritur, quomodo efficax sit probatio Apostoli ex verbis prædictis, quæ ad litteram de Salomone prædicta sunt, qui et vocatus est Amabilis Domino, ut patet intuenti seriem textus illius. Probatio autem fidei per auctoritatem Scripturæ, non valet nisi ex sensu litterali, secundum Augustinum in locis diversis. Et respondendum, quod verba hæc dicta sunt de Salomone in quantum erat figura Christi : ideo principaliter intelliguntur de Christo.
paras.en: According to the Gloss (and it is a gloss of Chrysostom), this testimony now alleged by the Apostle is taken from Isaias[[Is 42:1||]]: which, however, our translation does not have as to the form of the words. But as to the sense, we may say that it is taken from what is found there, according to the citation of Matthew the Evangelist: [[Matt 12:18|Behold my servant whom I have chosen|Ecce puer meus electus quem elegi]], etc. It seems more probable, however, that it is taken from the second book of Kings and the first of Paralipomenon[[2 Kings 7:14||]][[1 Par 17:13||]], where these words are contained in their proper form. But then a doubt arises, how the Apostle's proof from these words can hold, since they were spoken literally of Solomon, who was also called [[2 Kings 12:25|Amiable to the Lord|Amabilis Domino]], as is plain to anyone who looks at the course of that text. And a proof of the faith from the authority of Scripture is valid only from the literal sense, according to Augustine in various places. And the answer is that these words were said of Solomon inasmuch as he was a figure of Christ: therefore they are understood principally of Christ.

paras.t: Insuper ponit Apostolus aliam auctoritatem ad idem, videlicet quod Christus major sit angelis. Et quum iterum introducit, id est, quum Deus Pater introducendum seu adventurum rursus in Psalmo prænuntiat, primogenitum suum, id est Filium suum ante omnia genitum (qui in Proverbiis testatur : Dominus possedit me in initio viarum suarum, antequam quidquam faceret a principio), in orbem terræ dicit per Prophetam in Psalmo : Et adorent eum, videlicet Filium, omnes angeli Dei. Adoratio autem non convenit nisi Deo. Hac ergo auctoritate ostenditur Christus verus Deus, quem Deus Pater vult ab angelis adorari. Quoniam vero Apostolus dicit, Et quum iterum introducit, etc., quidam volunt solum de secundo Christi adventu hanc scripturam intelligi ; sed hoc non est necessarium : Primo, quoniam sensus est, Quum iterum introducit, id est, rursus introducendum prænuntiat : hoc enim frequenter prædixit. Secundo : nam ante adventum Christi in carnem, seu ante incarnationem introductus fuit in orbem terræ, id est in corda hominum per invisibilem missionem seu spiritualem adventum, ideo in sua incarnatione iterum introductus asseritur.
paras.en: Moreover the Apostle sets down another authority to the same end, namely that Christ is greater than the angels. [[1:6|And again, when he bringeth in|Et quum iterum introducit]], that is, when God the Father again foretells in the Psalm that he is to be brought in, or is to come, his [[1:6|first begotten|primogenitum]], that is, his Son begotten before all things (who testifies in Proverbs: [[Prov 8:22|The Lord possessed me in the beginning of his ways, before he made any thing from the beginning|Dominus possedit me in initio viarum suarum, antequam quidquam faceret a principio]]), [[1:6|into the world|in orbem terræ]], [[1:6|he saith|dicit]] by the Prophet in the Psalm: [[1:6|And let all the angels of God adore him|Et adorent eum, videlicet Filium, omnes angeli Dei]], namely the Son. But adoration belongs to God alone. By this authority, then, Christ is shown to be true God, whom God the Father wills to be adored by the angels. But since the Apostle says, [[1:6|And again, when he bringeth in|Et quum iterum introducit]], etc., some will have this scripture understood only of the second coming of Christ; but this is not necessary. First, because the sense is: [[1:6|again, when he bringeth in|Quum iterum introducit]], that is, he again foretells that he is to be brought in: for this he foretold often. Secondly, because before Christ's coming in the flesh, that is, before the incarnation, he was brought into the world, that is, into the hearts of men, by an invisible mission or spiritual coming; therefore in his incarnation he is said to be brought in *again*.

paras.t: Et ad angelos quidem dicit, id est, de conditione et existentia angelorum Dominus loquitur per Prophetam in Psalmo : Qui Deus Pater, seu Filius secundum quod Deus, facit angelos suos spiritus, id est, spirituales et intellectuales substantias facit suos legatos, dum eos ad aliqua nuntianda seu operanda emittit. Angelus enim est nomen officii, spiritus nomen naturæ : quemadmodum miles est nomen officii, homo nomen naturæ. Quemadmodum ergo homo fit miles, non e contrario : sic Deus spirituales illas substantias, quæ ex creatione sunt spiritus, efficit angelos, id est nuntios, injungendo eis obsequium. Et ministros suos flammam ignis, id est, angelos de ordine Seraphim, qui ob divini amoris fervorem flamma ignis ignisque urens vocantur, facit Deus ministros suos, ita quod ipsi quoque ministri sunt, non filii per naturam, nec veri dii. Vel per flammam ignis omnes angeli designantur, propter suæ naturæ agilitatem, suique motus velocitatem, et quia divinæ caritatis calore succensi sunt. De quibus exponi potest illud Danielis : Thronus ejus, videlicet Dei, flammæ ignis ; rotæ ejus, ignis accensus.
paras.en: [[1:7|And to the angels indeed he saith|Et ad angelos quidem dicit]], that is, of the condition and being of the angels the Lord speaks by the Prophet in the Psalm: [[1:7|He that|Qui]], God the Father, or the Son as God, [[1:7|maketh his angels spirits|facit angelos suos spiritus]], that is, he makes spiritual and intellectual substances his envoys, when he sends them out to announce or to do something [Denis takes it as "he maketh spirits his angels", that is, his messengers]. For *angel* is the name of an office, *spirit* the name of a nature: as *soldier* is the name of an office, *man* the name of a nature. As, then, a man becomes a soldier, and not the other way round, so God makes those spiritual substances, which by their creation are spirits, angels, that is, messengers, by laying a service upon them. [[1:7|And his ministers a flame of fire|Et ministros suos flammam ignis]], that is, the angels of the order of Seraphim, who because of the fervour of divine love are called a flame of fire and a burning fire, God makes his ministers, so that they too are ministers, not sons by nature, nor true gods. Or by *a flame of fire* all the angels are signified, because of the nimbleness of their nature and the swiftness of their motion, and because they are kindled with the heat of divine charity. Of them may be expounded that saying of Daniel: [[Dan 7:9|his throne|Thronus ejus]], that is, God's, [[Dan 7:9|like flames of fire: the wheels of it like a burning fire|flammæ ignis ; rotæ ejus, ignis accensus]].

paras.t: Porro quod dictum est, Adorent eum, etc., nostra translatio sic habet : Adorate eum, omnes angeli ejus. Similiter quod subditur, Qui facit angelos suos, etc., sic continet : Qui facis angelos tuos spiritus, et ministros tuos ignem urentem. Christus enim atque Apostoli sæpe allegant Scripturas potius quantum ad sensum, quam secundum formam verborum.
paras.en: Further, where it is said, [[1:6|adore him|Adorent eum]], etc., our translation [that is, the Latin psalter in use] has it thus: [[Ps 96:7|Adore him, all you his angels|Adorate eum, omnes angeli ejus]]. Likewise where it follows, [[1:7|He that maketh his angels|Qui facit angelos suos]], etc., it reads thus: [[Ps 103:4|Who makest thy angels spirits: and thy ministers a burning fire|Qui facis angelos tuos spiritus, et ministros tuos ignem urentem]]. For Christ and the Apostles often allege the Scriptures according to the sense rather than according to the form of the words.

paras.t: Ad Filium autem Dominus ait per Prophetam : Thronus tuus, id est regia dignitas, judiciaria potestas, et sedes qua resides ad dexteram Patris, o Deus Fili, in sæculum sæculi, id est, æternaliter permanet. Hoc de Christo secundum utramque naturam intelligi potest. Nam Pater omne judicium dedit Filio, deditque ei potestatem et judicium facere, quia Filius hominis est, et omnia ei subjecit. Secundum divinitatem vero, convenit Christo judiciaria potestas et regia dignitas per auctoritatem, quamvis receperit ea a Patre : imo una numero est potestas dignitasque amborum. Et virga æquitatis, id est regula justa et æqua disciplina, est virga regni tui, id est gubernatio et disciplina qua Ecclesiam regis et instruis, malosque percutis et justos exaltas. Potest quoque per virgam hanc accipi doctrina et lex christiana, per quam regnum Christi, id est Ecclesia militans, regitur, edocetur, atque corrigitur. De hac virga ait Psalmista : Reges eos in virga ferrea ; et Isaias, Percutiet (inquit) terram virga oris sui.
paras.en: [[1:8|But to the Son|Ad Filium autem]] the Lord says by the Prophet: [[1:8|Thy throne|Thronus tuus]][[Ps 44:7||]], that is, the royal dignity, the judicial power, and the seat in which thou sittest at the right hand of the Father, [[1:8|O God|o Deus]] the Son, [[1:8|is for ever and ever|in sæculum sæculi]], that is, abides eternally. This may be understood of Christ according to both natures. For the Father [[John 5:22|hath given all judgment to the Son|omne judicium dedit Filio]], [[John 5:27|and he hath given him power to do judgment, because he is the Son of man|deditque ei potestatem et judicium facere, quia Filius hominis est]], and has subjected all things to him. But according to his Godhead, judicial power and royal dignity belong to Christ by authority [that is, as his own, not as delegated], although he received them from the Father: nay, the power and dignity of both are numerically one. [[1:8|A sceptre of justice|Et virga æquitatis]] [*virga* means both "sceptre" and "rod"], that is, a just rule and equitable discipline, [[1:8|is the sceptre of thy kingdom|est virga regni tui]], that is, the government and discipline by which thou rulest and instructest the Church, and strikest the wicked and exaltest the just. By this sceptre may also be understood the Christian doctrine and law, by which the kingdom of Christ, that is, the Church militant, is ruled, taught and corrected. Of this rod the Psalmist says: [[Ps 2:9|Thou shalt rule them with a rod of iron|Reges eos in virga ferrea]]; and Isaias: [[Is 11:4|he shall strike|Percutiet]] (he says) [[Is 11:4|the earth with the rod of his mouth|terram virga oris sui]].

paras.t: Dilexisti justitiam, id est omnem virtutem et omne bonum : justitia enim est omnis virtus ; et odisti iniquitatem. Propterea, id est merito hujus, videlicet quoniam sic fecisti, unxit te, o Christe, Deus omnium, qui est Deus tuus specialiter secundum quod homo es. Tamen secundum Augustinum, in Græco est manifesta distinctio casuum, ut primum quod dicitur, Deus, sit vocativi casus, aliud nominativi. Eritque sensus : Propterea unxit te, o Deus Fili, Deus tuus, id est Deus Pater. Unxit itaque te secundum humanam naturam, oleo exsultationis, id est præmio accidentali, videlicet corporis glorificatione, ascensione, et plena lætitia partis sensitivæ, quæ usque ad horam mortis tuæ passibilis fuit, præ participibus tuis, id est præ cunctis electis, qui membra tua sunt, et de plenitudine tua accipiunt, vel una tecum a supersancta Trinitate gratiam et gloriam sortiuntur. Vel sic : Propterea, id est, ut justitiam diligeres, et iniquitatem odires, unxit te, Deus, Deus tuus, oleo exsultationis, id est lenitate ac plenitudine gratiæ animam exhilarantis, in sacerdotem, pontificem, regem, prophetam, ac pugilem. Unde per Isaiam Christus testatur : Spiritus Domini super me, eo quod unxerit me.
paras.en: [[1:9|Thou hast loved justice|Dilexisti justitiam]][[Ps 44:8||]], that is, all virtue and all good: for justice is every virtue; [[1:9|and hated iniquity|et odisti iniquitatem]]. [[1:9|Therefore|Propterea]], that is, by the merit of this, namely because thou hast done so, [[1:9|hath anointed thee|unxit te]], O Christ, the God of all, who is [[1:9|thy God|Deus tuus]] in a special way according as thou art man. Yet according to Augustine, in the Greek there is a plain distinction of cases, so that the first *God* is in the vocative case, the other in the nominative. And the sense will be: *Therefore, O God* the Son, *thy God*, that is, God the Father, *hath anointed thee*. He has anointed thee, then, according to thy human nature, [[1:9|with the oil of gladness|oleo exsultationis]], that is, with the accidental reward [that is, joys added to the essential reward, which is the vision of God], namely the glorifying of thy body, the ascension, and the full gladness of the sensitive part, which until the hour of thy death was passible, [[1:9|above thy fellows|præ participibus tuis]], that is, above all the elect, who are thy members and receive of thy fulness[[John 1:16||]], or who together with thee receive grace and glory from the all-holy Trinity. Or thus: [[1:9|therefore|Propterea]], that is, that thou mightest love justice and hate iniquity, [[1:9|God, thy God, hath anointed thee with the oil of gladness|unxit te, Deus, Deus tuus, oleo exsultationis]], that is, with the gentleness and fulness of grace that gladdens the soul, to be priest, pontiff, king, prophet and champion. Hence Christ testifies by Isaias: [[Is 61:1|The spirit of the Lord is upon me, because the Lord hath anointed me|Spiritus Domini super me, eo quod unxerit me]].

paras.t: Consequenter probat Apostolus Filium Patri coæternum. Et : Tu in principio temporis, id est simul cum tempore, Domine Fili ; vel, Tu, Domine Pater, in principio, id est in Filio, seu per Filium, per quem omnia agis (qui ait : Ego principium, qui et loquor vobis); terram fundasti, id est creasti et firmiter collocasti in medio universi ; et opera manuum tuarum sunt cœli omnes. Manus autem Dei, dicuntur intellectus ejus practicus et voluntas, quibus omnia producuntur.
paras.en: Next the Apostle proves the Son coeternal with the Father. [[1:10|And: Thou in the beginning|Et : Tu in principio]][[Ps 101:26||]] of time, that is, together with time, [[1:10|O Lord|Domine]] the Son; or, *Thou, O Lord* the Father, *in the beginning*, that is, in the Son, or through the Son, through whom thou doest all things (who says: [[John 8:25|The beginning, who also speak unto you|Ego principium, qui et loquor vobis]]); [[1:10|didst found the earth|terram fundasti]], that is, didst create it and set it firmly in the midst of the universe; [[1:10|and the works of thy hands are the heavens|et opera manuum tuarum sunt cœli]], all of them. Now the hands of God are said to be his practical intellect and his will, by which all things are brought forth.

paras.t: Ipsi, id est cœli, peribunt, quantum ad esse accidentale, non quantum ad substantiam. Motus namque et influentia et qualitas eorum cessabunt. Tu autem permanebis, id est, incommutabiliter in te ipso subsistes : apud quem non est permutatio, nec vicissitudinis obumbratio ; qui asseris, Ego Dominus, et non mutor. Et omnes cœli ut vestimentum veterascent, quantum ad modum essendi quem nunc habent. Præterit quippe figura hujus mundi. Et Christus in Evangelio : Cœlum, ait, et terra transibunt. Et velut amictum, id est vestem, mutabis eos, id est, a solito cursu et influxu cessare facies, et mutabuntur a pristina qualitate, atque in melius commutabuntur : quemadmodum dictum est plenius ad Romanos. Unde in Apocalypsi habetur : Vidi cœlum novum et terram novam ; primum enim cœlum et prima terra abiit. Et per Isaiam Dominus : Ecce, inquit, ego creo cœlos novos et terram novam, et non erunt in memoria priora. Tu autem idem ipse es, id est, penitus incommutabilis es, et anni tui non deficient, id est, æternitas tua omne tempus comprehendens, et tuum esse mensurans, non finietur.
paras.en: [[1:11|They|Ipsi]], that is, the heavens, [[1:11|shall perish|peribunt]], as to their accidental being, not as to their substance. For their motion and influence and quality will cease. [[1:11|But thou shalt continue|Tu autem permanebis]], that is, thou shalt subsist unchangeably in thyself: thou [[Jas 1:17|with whom there is no change nor shadow of alteration|apud quem non est permutatio, nec vicissitudinis obumbratio]]; who declarest: [[Mal 3:6|I am the Lord, and I change not|Ego Dominus, et non mutor]]. [[1:11|And they shall all|Et omnes]], the heavens, [[1:11|grow old as a garment|ut vestimentum veterascent]], as to the manner of being which they now have. [[1 Cor 7:31|For the fashion of this world passeth away|Præterit quippe figura hujus mundi]]. And Christ in the Gospel: [[Matt 24:35|Heaven|Cœlum]], he says, [[Matt 24:35|and earth shall pass|et terra transibunt]]. [[1:12|And as a vesture|Et velut amictum]], that is, a garment, [[1:12|shalt thou change them|mutabis eos]], that is, thou shalt make them cease from their wonted course and influence, [[1:12|and they shalt be changed|et mutabuntur]] from their former quality, and shall be changed for the better: as was said more fully on the Romans[[Rom 8:22||]] [that is, in Denis's commentary on that epistle]. Hence it is said in the Apocalypse: [[Apoc 21:1|I saw a new heaven and a new earth. For the first heaven and the first earth was gone|Vidi cœlum novum et terram novam ; primum enim cœlum et prima terra abiit]]. And the Lord by Isaias: [[Is 65:17|behold|Ecce]], he says, [[Is 65:17|I create new heavens, and a new earth: and the former things shall not be in remembrance|ego creo cœlos novos et terram novam, et non erunt in memoria priora]]. [[1:12|But thou art the selfsame|Tu autem idem ipse es]], that is, thou art wholly unchangeable, [[1:12|and thy years shall not fail|et anni tui non deficient]], that is, thy eternity, which contains all time and measures thy being, shall not come to an end.

paras.t: Rursus auctoritate Psalmistæ probatur excellentia Christi præ angelis. Ad quem autem angelorum dixit Deus Pater aliquando, Sede a dextris meis (secundum sensum jam explicatum), quoadusque ponam inimicos tuos scabellum pedum tuorum, id est, plene eos tibi subjiciam? tanquam dicat : Nulli angelorum dictum est hoc, quod tamen Pater ait ad Filium : cui dixit Pater in ascensione, ut sedeat secum usque ad diem judicii, in quo omnes inimici Christi, videlicet reprobi, Christo perfectissime subjicientur quantum ad suæ dominationis exsecutionem, quamvis et nunc ei subjecti sint quantum ad suæ potestatis auctoritatem. Per hoc autem quod dicitur, Quoadusque, vel, Donec, non datur intelligi quod postea non sedebit.
paras.en: Again, by the authority of the Psalmist the excellence of Christ above the angels is proved. [[1:13|But to which of the angels said he|Ad quem autem angelorum dixit]], God the Father, [[1:13|at any time|aliquando]]: [[1:13|Sit on my right hand|Sede a dextris meis]] (in the sense already explained), [[1:13|until I make thy enemies thy footstool|quoadusque ponam inimicos tuos scabellum pedum tuorum]][[Ps 109:1||]], that is, until I fully subject them to thee? As if to say: To none of the angels was this said, which yet the Father says to the Son: to whom the Father said at the ascension that he should sit with him until the day of judgment, in which all the enemies of Christ, namely the reprobate, will be most perfectly subjected to Christ as to the carrying out of his dominion, although even now they are subject to him as to the authority of his power. But by what is said, *until*, or *till*, it is not given to be understood that afterwards he will not sit.

paras.t: Nonne omnes angeli sunt administratorii spiritus, id est divino imperio servientes, in ministerium, id est ad obsequium seu adjutorium electorum, missi a Deo, missione interiori vel exteriori, propter eos, id est eorum profectum, qui hereditatem capiunt salutis, id est, cœlestem atque beatam hereditatem patriæ, scilicet beatificam Dei visionem, adipiscuntur ?
paras.en: [[1:14|Are they not all ministering spirits|Nonne omnes angeli sunt administratorii spiritus]], that is, serving the divine command, [[1:14|to minister|in ministerium]], that is, for the service or help of the elect, [[1:14|sent|missi]] by God, by an interior or exterior mission, [[1:14|for them|propter eos]], that is, for their advancement, [[1:14|who shall receive the inheritance of salvation|qui hereditatem capiunt salutis]], that is, who obtain the heavenly and blessed inheritance of the fatherland, namely the beatific vision of God?

paras.t: Quæri hic potest, an omnes angeli foras mittantur. Et videtur quod sic, auctoritate Apostoli loco præsenti ; item ex eo quod ab Isaia dicitur, Volavit ad me unus de Seraphim. Multi quoque Sanctorum videntur hoc dicere. Hanc quæstionem Gregorius non præsumit nec audet determinare. Quidam vero dixerunt, quod secundum communem legem, et ut plurimum atque ex proprio officio, soli inferiores mittuntur ad extra. Superiores tamen interdum ex speciali ratione et divina dispensatione mittuntur.
paras.en: It may be asked here whether all the angels are sent outward. And it seems that they are, by the authority of the Apostle in the present place; and also from what is said by Isaias: [[Is 6:6|one of the seraphims flew to me|Volavit ad me unus de Seraphim]]. Many of the Saints, too, seem to say this. This question Gregory does not presume or dare to settle. Some, however, have said that by the common law, and for the most part, and by their proper office, only the lower angels are sent outward; yet the higher are sometimes sent, for a special reason and by divine dispensation.

paras.t: Sed hanc responsionem improbat S. Thomas in prima parte. Nam ordo angelorum attenditur secundum dona gratiarum. Ordo autem gratiæ summus est : idcirco non habet ordinem superiorem propter quem omittatur : quemadmodum ordo naturæ prætermittitur propter ordinem gratiæ, quatenus gratia declaratur, seu fides confirmetur, ut patet in suscitatione defuncti. Ad fidei autem confirmationem non proficeret omissio gratiæ, quum non percipiatur a nobis. Denique, nullum ministerium adeo magnum est, quod per inferiores expleri non valeat, quia secundum Gregorium, archangeli appellantur, qui summa annuntiant. Insuper, nulla persona viatoris præstantior est Maria, nullum quoque ministerium majus est annuntiatione Filii Dei : et tamen ad beatissimam Virginem pro hoc summo negotio missus est angelus Gabriel, qui est de secundo ordine infimæ hierarchiæ. Ex his concludit sanctus Doctor, quod angeli superiores nunquam ad exterius ministerium destinentur. Et hoc verius reor, præsertim propter hoc quoniam dictis divini Dionysii potius consonat. Dicit quoque B. Dionysius quod angelus missus ad Isaiam, non erat de ordine Seraphim, sed unus de inferioribus. Dicitur vero unus de Seraphim, vel quoniam missus ab uno de ordine Seraphim, vel ratione sui effectus, quia labia Prophetæ incendendo purgavit.
paras.en: But St Thomas rejects this answer in the First Part [of the *Summa*]. For the order of the angels is reckoned according to the gifts of grace. And the order of grace is the highest: therefore it has no higher order for whose sake it should be set aside, as the order of nature is passed over for the sake of the order of grace, so that grace may be made known or faith confirmed, as is plain in the raising of the dead. But the setting aside of grace would do nothing to confirm faith, since it is not perceived by us. Further, no ministry is so great that it cannot be fulfilled by the lower angels, since, according to Gregory, those are called archangels who announce the highest things. Moreover, no wayfarer [that is, no one still in this life] is more excellent than Mary, and no ministry is greater than the annunciation of the Son of God: and yet to the most blessed Virgin, for this highest business, [[Luke 1:26|the angel Gabriel was sent|missus est angelus Gabriel]], who is of the second order of the lowest hierarchy. From these things the holy Doctor concludes that the higher angels are never appointed to an outward ministry. And this I think the truer, especially because it agrees better with the words of the divine Dionysius. Blessed Dionysius also says that the angel sent to Isaias[[Is 6:6||]] [the margin gives only Is. vi] was not of the order of Seraphim, but one of the lower angels. He is called one of the Seraphim either because he was sent by one of the order of Seraphim, or by reason of his effect, because he purged the Prophet's lips by burning them.

paras.t: Dicit etiam Thomas, quod sicut divinis Personis, videlicet Filio et Spiritui Sancto, attribuitur duplex missio, utputa invisibilis, propter gratiæ infusionem, atque visibilis, propter creaturam corporalem assumptam vel manifestatam, sic angelis convenit duplex missio, scilicet : interior, secundum operationes intellectuales, prout unus illuminat alium. Sicque superiores mittuntur, medios et inferiores illustrando, et ad exteriora officia dirigendo ordine hierarchico. Alia est eorum exterior missio, secundum actus transeuntes circa corpoream creaturam. Sic soli inferiores mittuntur. Omnes ergo sunt administratorii spiritus, in ministerium missi missione interiori vel exteriori. Quatuor autem superiores ordines non mittuntur ad extra, secundum Thomam, sed quandoque inferiores, videlicet Angeli, Archangeli, Principatus, Potestates, Virtutes.
paras.en: Thomas also says that, as a twofold mission is attributed to the divine Persons, namely to the Son and the Holy Ghost, an invisible one, by the infusion of grace, and a visible one, by a bodily creature assumed or shown, so a twofold mission belongs to the angels: an interior one, by intellectual operations, as one enlightens another; and in this way the higher angels are sent, enlightening the middle and the lower and directing them to outward offices in hierarchical order. The other is their exterior mission, by transient acts [that is, acts that pass outside the agent] upon bodily creatures; and in this way only the lower angels are sent. They are, then, [[1:14|all ministering spirits, sent to minister|Omnes ergo sunt administratorii spiritus, in ministerium missi]] by an interior or exterior mission. But the four higher orders are not sent outward, according to Thomas, but sometimes [the text reads *quandoque*, "sometimes"; perhaps read *quinque*, "the five", since five orders are named] the lower ones, namely Angels, Archangels, Principalities, Powers, Virtues.

2.title: EXPLANATIO CAPITULI SECUNDI : PROPTEREA ABUNDANTIUS OPORTET OBSERVARE NOS, ETC.
2.title_en: Explanation of the second chapter: Therefore ought we more diligently to observe, etc.

paras.t: Declarata excellentia Christi, consequenter ostenditur cum quanta diligentia observanda sit doctrina et lex tanti magistri. Propterea, id est, quum tanta sit dignitas Christi legislatoris nostri, abundantius, id est multum reverenter et timorate, vel copiosius atque perfectius quam a Judæis observata fuit lex Moysis, oportet, id est, ad salutem necessarium est, observare nos, sæpius recolendo et fortiter adimplendo, ea quæ audivimus a Christo mediate vel immediate, qui et quotidie loquitur nobis per Evangelium, ne forte pereffluamus, id est, penitus pereamus et in æternum damnemur. Fluimus quippe per peccata venialia et mortalis naturæ quotidiana tormenta, sicut Job ait: Homo natus de muliere, brevi vivens tempore, repletur multis miseriis, et nunquam in eodem statu permanet. Propter quod ait Scriptura: Omnes morimur et quasi aquæ dilabimur in terram, quæ non revertuntur. Effluimus autem per peccata mortalia; sed pereffluamus, id est, perfecte effluimus, incidendo æterna cruciamenta.
paras.en: Having set forth the excellence of Christ, he next shows with what diligence the teaching and the law of so great a master are to be observed. [[2:1|Therefore|Propterea]], that is, since the dignity of Christ our lawgiver is so great, [[2:1|more diligently|abundantius]], that is, with much reverence and fear, or more abundantly and more perfectly than the law of Moses was observed by the Jews, [[2:1|ought we|oportet]], that is, it is necessary for salvation, [[2:1|to observe|observare nos]], by often recalling them and steadfastly fulfilling them, [[2:1|the things which we have heard|ea quæ audivimus]] from Christ, mediately or immediately, who also speaks to us daily through the Gospel, [[2:1|lest perhaps we should let them slip|ne forte pereffluamus]] [the Latin *pereffluamus* means "flow away utterly"; Denis plays on *fluimus*, "we flow", *effluimus*, "we flow out", and *pereffluamus*], that is, lest we perish utterly and be damned for ever. For we flow through venial sins and the daily torments of our mortal nature, as Job says: [[Job 14:1|Man born of a woman, living for a short time, is filled with many miseries|Homo natus de muliere, brevi vivens tempore, repletur multis miseriis]], [[Job 14:2|and never continueth in the same state|et nunquam in eodem statu permanet]]. For which reason the Scripture says: [[2 Kings 14:14|We all die, and like waters that return no more, we fall down into the earth|Omnes morimur et quasi aquæ dilabimur in terram, quæ non revertuntur]]. But we flow out through mortal sins; and we *flow away utterly*, that is, we flow out completely, when we fall into eternal torments.

paras.t: Quod ergo tam diligenter servanda sint verba Christi, probat Apostolus per locum a minori. Si enim qui per angelos dictus est sermo, id est, quia doctrina Dei, ministerio angelorum tradita Moysi: prout Stephanus dixit, Accepistis legem in dispositione angelorum; factus est firmus, id est, rate severeque injuncta ac firmiter servata est, et multipliciter confirmata miraculis, minis, pœnis, atque promissis; et omnis prævaricatio, id est legis transgressio, mala committendo, et inobedientia, id est incustodia præceptorum, bona omittendo: quorum primum est contra præcepta negativa, secundum contra præcepta affirmativa; accepit justam mercedis retributionem, id est debitam pœnam, tempore veteris Testamenti in populo Judæorum, quemadmodum Moyses scripsit: Pro mensura peccati erit et plagarum modus. Quum ergo sit ita, quomodo nos Christiani effugiemus ultionem divinæ justitiæ, si tantam neglexerimus salutem, id est, tam salutarem Christi doctrinam, tam copiosam ejus gratiam, tantam beatitudinem nobis ab eo promissam parvi penderimus et obliti fuerimus?
paras.en: That the words of Christ are to be kept so diligently, the Apostle proves by an argument from the lesser. [[2:2|For if the word spoken by angels|Si enim qui per angelos dictus est sermo]], that is, the teaching of God handed down to Moses by the ministry of angels, as Stephen said: You [[Acts 7:53|have received the law by the disposition of angels|Accepistis legem in dispositione angelorum]]; [[2:2|became steadfast|factus est firmus]], that is, was validly and sternly enjoined and firmly kept, and confirmed in many ways by miracles, threats, punishments and promises[[Mark 16:20||]]; [[2:2|and every transgression|et omnis prævaricatio]], that is, transgression of the law by doing evil, [[2:2|and disobedience|et inobedientia]], that is, failure to keep the commandments by leaving good undone (the first of these is against the negative precepts, the second against the affirmative precepts), [[2:2|received a just recompense of reward|accepit justam mercedis retributionem]], that is, due punishment, in the time of the Old Testament among the Jewish people, as Moses wrote: [[Deut 25:2|According to the measure of the sin shall the measure also of the stripes be|Pro mensura peccati erit et plagarum modus]]. Since, then, this is so, [[2:3|How shall we|quomodo nos]] Christians [[2:3|escape|effugiemus]] the vengeance of divine justice, [[2:3|if we neglect so great salvation|si tantam neglexerimus salutem]], that is, if we make little of and forget so saving a teaching of Christ, so plentiful a grace of his, so great a beatitude promised us by him?

paras.t: Quæ salus quum initium accepisset enarrari per Dominum, id est, quum a Christo cœpta est prædicari, ab eis qui audierunt, id est ab ore Apostolorum, qui cum Christo corporaliter conversati sunt, ejusque sermonibus interfuerunt: quibus et dictum est, Vobis datum est nosse mysterium regni Dei; et, Beati oculi qui vident quæ vos videtis; in nos confirmata est, id est, nobis firmiter annuntiata atque ingesta est. Hoc dicit Apostolus in persona fidelium, non sui: ipse enim a Christo immediate edoctus fuit in raptu. Unde ad Galatas loquitur: Mihi qui videbantur esse aliquid (videlicet Petrus, Jacobus et Joannes), nihil contulerunt.
paras.en: [[2:3|Which, having begun to be declared by the Lord|Quæ salus quum initium accepisset enarrari per Dominum]], that is, when it began to be preached by Christ, [[2:3|by them that heard him|ab eis qui audierunt]], that is, from the mouth of the Apostles, who lived in bodily presence with Christ and were present at his discourses, to whom it was also said: [[Mark 4:11|To you it is given to know the mystery of the kingdom of God|Vobis datum est nosse mysterium regni Dei]]; and: [[Luke 10:23|Blessed are the eyes that see the things which you see|Beati oculi qui vident quæ vos videtis]]; [[2:3|was confirmed unto us|in nos confirmata est]], that is, was firmly announced and brought home to us. The Apostle says this in the person of the faithful, not in his own: for he himself was taught by Christ immediately, in his rapture[[2 Cor 12:4||]]. Hence he says to the Galatians: [[Gal 2:6|for to me they that seemed to be some thing|Mihi qui videbantur esse aliquid]] (namely Peter, James and John) [[Gal 2:6|added nothing|nihil contulerunt]].

paras.t: Confirmata est ergo hæc salus in nos, contestante, id est prædicationi Apostolorum testimonium perhibente, Deo, qui neminem fallit, signis, id est per minora miracula, quæ quantum ad substantiam facti, fieri possunt per naturam, non tamen quoad modum fiendi, sicut est quarumdam infirmitatum depulsio, quæ fieri potest a medicis, et portentis, id est per majora miracula, quæ sunt omnino supra naturam, ut est suscitatio mortui, et variis virtutibus, id est potentissimis Dei effectibus, quæ non solum naturalem cursum, sed etiam rationem humanam excedunt, ut est penetratio dimensionum; vel, variis virtutibus, id est habitibus virtuosis atque infusis, videlicet fide, spe, caritate, donisque Spiritus Sancti; et Spiritus Sancti distributionibus, id est gratiis gratis datis a Spiritu, de quibus dictum Corinthiis jam est: Alii datur per Spiritum sermo sapientiæ, alii sermo scientiæ, alii genera linguarum, alii discretio spiritum: quæ primo datæ sunt sanctis Apostolis in die Pentecostes, et per eos datæ sunt aliis multis, ut legitur in Actibus Apostolorum. Quæ omnia facta et data sunt secundum suam voluntatem, id est ex beneplacito Dei, qui omnia operatur secundum propositum voluntatis suæ, non secundum merita hominum. Alioqui gratia jam non esset gratia.
paras.en: This salvation, then, was confirmed unto us, [[2:4|bearing them witness|contestante]], that is, bearing witness to the preaching of the Apostles, [[2:4|God|Deo]], who deceives no one, [[2:4|by signs|signis]], that is, by lesser miracles, which as to the substance of the deed can be done by nature, though not as to the manner of doing it, such as the driving out of certain sicknesses, which physicians can do; [[2:4|and wonders|et portentis]], that is, by greater miracles, which are wholly above nature, such as the raising of the dead; [[2:4|and divers miracles|et variis virtutibus]], that is, by most mighty works of God, which surpass not only the course of nature but human reason too, such as the passing of one body through another [penetratio dimensionum, that is, two bodies in one place, as when Christ came in to the disciples through closed doors]; or, [[2:4|divers miracles|variis virtutibus]] [the Latin *virtutes* means both "miracles" and "virtues"], that is, virtuous and infused habits, namely faith, hope, charity and the gifts of the Holy Ghost; [[2:4|and distributions of the Holy Ghost|et Spiritus Sancti distributionibus]], that is, by the graces freely given [gratiæ gratis datæ, that is, gifts given for the good of others, not for the sanctifying of the one who receives them] by the Spirit, of which it has already been said to the Corinthians: [[1 Cor 12:8|To one indeed, by the Spirit, is given the word of wisdom: and to another, the word of knowledge|Alii datur per Spiritum sermo sapientiæ, alii sermo scientiæ]], [[1 Cor 12:10|to another, diverse kinds of tongues|alii genera linguarum]], [[1 Cor 12:10|to another, the discerning of spirits|alii discretio spiritum]]: which were given first to the holy Apostles on the day of Pentecost[[Acts 2:4||]], and through them were given to many others, as we read in the Acts of the Apostles[[Acts 8:17||]][[Acts 10:44||]][[Acts 19:6||]]. All these were done and given [[2:4|according to his own will|secundum suam voluntatem]], that is, by the good pleasure of God, who [[Eph 1:11|worketh all things according to the counsel of his will|omnia operatur secundum propositum voluntatis suæ]], not according to the merits of men. Otherwise [[Rom 11:6|grace is no more grace|gratia jam non esset gratia]].

paras.t: Hæc sunt christianæ fidei argumenta. Incomprehensibilis namque supernaturalisque veritas, supernaturalibus atque divinis eguit argumentis. Unde et in Evangelio scribitur: Illi profecti prædicaverunt ubique, Domino cooperante et sermonem confirmante sequentibus signis. Hinc in Joannis epistola scriptum est: Qui non credit in Filium, mendacem facit Patrem, quoniam non credit in testimonium quod testificatus est Deus de Filio suo. De quo testimonio ait et Filius: Opera quæ dedit mihi Pater, etc., testimonium perhibent de me.
paras.en: These are the proofs of the Christian faith. For a truth incomprehensible and supernatural needed supernatural and divine proofs. Hence it is written in the Gospel too: [[Mark 16:20|they going forth preached every where: the Lord working withal, and confirming the word with signs that followed|Illi profecti prædicaverunt ubique, Domino cooperante et sermonem confirmante sequentibus signis]]. Hence it is written in the epistle of John: [[1 John 5:10|He that believeth not the Son maketh him a liar: because he believeth not in the testimony which God hath testified of his Son|Qui non credit in Filium, mendacem facit Patrem, quoniam non credit in testimonium quod testificatus est Deus de Filio suo]]. Of which testimony the Son also says: [[John 5:36|the works which the Father hath given me|Opera quæ dedit mihi Pater]], etc., [[John 5:36|give testimony of me|testimonium perhibent de me]][[John 10:25||]].

paras.t: Quod autem non effugiemus ultionem divinam, si tantam neglexerimus salutem, probat Apostolus per hoc quod Christus sublimior est atque potentior angelis. Non enim angelis subjecit Deus orbem terræ futurum, id est orbem terræ seu mundum secundum statum quem habebit post diem judicii: quamvis interim aliquo modo subjectus sit eis, quoniam movent cœlestia corpora, quorum motu et influentia transmutantur hæc inferiora; de quo orbe terræ futuro loquimur. De orbe enim terræ quantum ad statum futurum, intendit Apostolus loqui. Oportet ergo advertere, quod quum omnia corporalia et terrena ordinentur ad hominem, sicut duplex est status seu perfectio hominis, una secundum suam institutionem in via hujus exsilii, alia secundum suam glorificationem in patria cœlesti; sic duplex est status orbis terræ seu mundi: unus, secundum successionem generationis et corruptionis, donec compleatur numerus electorum, qui dicitur status præsens, durans usque ad diem judicii; alius, secundum futuræ renovationis stabilitatem quæ fiet in die novissimo. Quamvis autem mundus seu orbis terræ in utroque statu sit substantialiter idem, tamen propter differentiam statuum dicitur orbis terræ præsens, et orbis terræ futurus. Quemadmodum autem homines, quantum ad statum præsentem, subjecti sunt angelis, quia reguntur, purgantur, illuminantur, ac perficiuntur ab eis, secundum Dionysium; quæ tamen prælatio in futuro statu cessabit, quantum ad novam influentiam: sic orbis terræ, secundum præsentem statum, angelis est subjectus, juxta modum prædictum: sed secundum statum futurum, eis non erit subjectus: tunc enim alterationes et generationes cessabunt. Hæc expositio videtur mihi textui magis conformis. Glossa tamen aliis modis exponit hunc locum: quam inspicere potest, qui alium sensum requirit.
paras.en: That we shall not escape the divine vengeance [[2:3|if we neglect so great salvation|si tantam neglexerimus salutem]], the Apostle proves from this, that Christ is higher and mightier than the angels. [[2:5|For God hath not subjected unto angels the world to come|Non enim angelis subjecit Deus orbem terræ futurum]], that is, the world or universe according to the state it will have after the day of judgement; though in the meantime it is in some way subject to them, since they move the heavenly bodies, by whose motion and influence these lower things are changed; [[2:5|whereof we speak|de quo orbe terræ futuro loquimur]]. For the Apostle means to speak of the world as to its future state. We must note, then, that since all bodily and earthly things are ordered to man, just as the state or perfection of man is twofold, one according to his first making, on the way of this exile, the other according to his glorification in the heavenly fatherland, so the state of the world or universe is twofold: one according to the succession of generation and corruption until the number of the elect is complete, which is called the present state and lasts until the day of judgement; the other according to the stability of the future renewal, which will take place on the last day. And although the world or universe is substantially the same in either state, yet because of the difference of the states it is called the present world and the world to come. Now just as men, as to the present state, are subject to the angels, since they are ruled, purged, enlightened and perfected by them, according to Dionysius (a rule which will nevertheless cease in the future state, as to any new influence), so the world, according to its present state, is subject to the angels in the way described; but according to its future state it will not be subject to them, for then alterations and generations will cease. This exposition seems to me more in keeping with the text. The Gloss, however, expounds this passage in other ways; whoever seeks another sense may consult it.

paras.t: Porro, quod Christo orbis futurus subjiciatur, probat Apostolus auctoritate Psalmistæ: Testatus est autem in quodam loco quis, id est quidam famosus, puta David propheta præclarus, dicens: Quid est homo, quicumque sit ille, quod memor es ejus, o Domine Deus omnipotens? tanquam dicat: Vilis et modicus est comparatione tuæ majestatis, quum sit corporalis, mortalis ac fragilis. Propter quod mirum est quod tam benigne dignaris eum respicere, adjuvare et sublimare, præsertim assumendo ejus naturam. Aut quid est filius hominis, id est Christus secundum humanam naturam assumptam, quoniam visitas eum, uniendo tuæ increatæ personalitati ejus humanitatem, et habitando in ea quasi in templo? quasi dicat: Hoc humanitati Christi ex sua naturali dignitate seu meritis non convenit.
paras.en: Further, that the world to come is subject to Christ, the Apostle proves by the authority of the Psalmist: [[2:6|But one in a certain place hath testified|Testatus est autem in quodam loco quis]], that is, someone famous, namely David, the renowned prophet[[Ps 8:5||]], [[2:6|saying|dicens]]: [[2:6|What is man|Quid est homo]], whoever he may be, [[2:6|that thou art mindful of him|quod memor es ejus]], O Lord God almighty? As if to say: He is vile and slight in comparison with thy majesty, since he is bodily, mortal and frail. Wherefore it is a wonder that thou deignest so kindly to look upon him, help him and raise him up, above all by taking on his nature. [[2:6|Or|Aut]] what is [[2:6|the son of man|filius hominis]], that is, Christ according to the human nature he assumed, [[2:6|that thou visitest him|quoniam visitas eum]], by uniting his humanity to thy uncreated personality [that is, to the divine Person of the Word, in which Christ's human nature subsists] and dwelling in it as in a temple? As if to say: This does not befit the humanity of Christ by its own natural dignity or merits.

paras.t: Minuisti eum paulo minus ab angelis: id est, quamvis Christum secundum humanitatem sic visitaveris atque sublimaveris, tamen quantum ad aliquid, fecisti eum angelis inferiorem, videlicet quoad corporis sui passibilitatem ac mortem, quæ angelis non conveniunt propter naturæ ipsorum excellentiam, quum sint immateriales essentiæ. Gloria et honore coronasti eum. Gloria, est clara cum laude notitia; honor vero, est exhibitio reverentiæ in signum virtutis. Deus ergo Pater seu Trinitas coronavit, id est, undique et multipliciter decoravit Christum hominem, gloria, infundendo cordibus hominum claram cognitionem excellentiæ Christi, et honore, inducendo fideles ad venerationem et cultum ipsius. Vel, Gloria, id est beatitudine animæ vel corporis glorificatione in resurrectione, et honore, id est elevatione ad dexteram tuam in ascensione, coronasti eum. Et constituisti eum super opera manuum tuarum, id est, omnibus creaturis eum præposuisti, faciens eum Regem regum et Dominum dominantium: quod post resurrectionem factum est quantum ad manifestationem.
paras.en: [[2:7|Thou hast made him a little lower than the angels|Minuisti eum paulo minus ab angelis]]: that is, although thou hast so visited and exalted Christ according to his humanity, yet in one respect thou hast made him lower than the angels, namely as to the passibility of his body, and his death, which do not befit the angels because of the excellence of their nature, since they are immaterial essences. [[2:7|thou hast crowned him with glory and honour|Gloria et honore coronasti eum]]. Glory is clear knowledge joined with praise; honour is the showing of reverence in token of virtue. God the Father, then, or the Trinity, crowned, that is, adorned on every side and in many ways, Christ the man, [[2:7|with glory|gloria]], by pouring into the hearts of men a clear knowledge of the excellence of Christ, [[2:7|and honour|et honore]], by bringing the faithful to venerate and worship him. Or: with glory, that is, with the beatitude of his soul, or with the glorifying of his body in the resurrection, and honour, that is, with his raising to thy right hand in the ascension, [[2:7|thou hast crowned him|coronasti eum]]. [[2:7|And hast set him over the works of thy hands|Et constituisti eum super opera manuum tuarum]], that is, thou hast set him over all creatures, making him [[Apoc 19:16|KING OF KINGS AND LORD OF LORDS|Regem regum et Dominum dominantium]]: which was done after the resurrection as to its manifestation.

paras.t: Omnia visibilia et invisibilia, suprema, media et infima, subjecisti sub pedibus ejus, id est, ei perfecte subdidisti quantum ad potestatis collationem, etiam ab exordio incarnationis. Tunc enim data est homini Christo potestas atque prælatio super universa creata. In eo autem quod Deus ei, videlicet Christo, omnia subjecit, nihil dimisit non subjectum ei, id est, universaliter sine exceptione cuncta ei subjecit. Verumtamen, quoniam nondum subjecta sunt ei omnia quantum ad potestatis exsecutionem et plenam manifestationem, subjungitur: Nunc autem, id est tempore isto usque ad diem judicii, necdum videmus omnia subjecta ei, quantum ad exsecutionem et plenam manifestationem: quod tamen fiet in die novissimo, quando juxta Isaiæ oraculum: Ad eum venient, et confundentur omnes qui repugnant ei. Nunc enim multi Christo resistunt, et nullam sentiunt pœnam: eum blasphemant vel inhonorant, et nullum experiuntur supplicium. Sed post diem judicii ita non erit. Extunc enim coacte erunt ei subjecti, pœnas luendo, qui nunc libere repugnant illi, impie conversando. Ideo convenienter prædictum est, futurum orbem Christo subjiciendum.
paras.en: [[2:8|Thou hast subjected all things|Omnia]], visible and invisible, highest, middle and lowest, [[2:8|under his feet|subjecisti sub pedibus ejus]], that is, thou hast perfectly subdued them to him as to the conferring of power, even from the beginning of the incarnation. For then power and authority over all created things was given to the man Christ[[Matt 28:18||]]. [[2:8|For in that|In eo autem quod]] God [[2:8|hath subjected all things to him|ei, videlicet Christo, omnia subjecit]], namely to Christ, [[2:8|he left nothing not subject to him|nihil dimisit non subjectum ei]], that is, he subjected all things to him universally, without exception. Yet, since all things are not yet subject to him as to the exercise of his power and its full manifestation, it is added: [[2:8|But now|Nunc autem]], that is, in this time until the day of judgement, [[2:8|we see not as yet all things subject to him|necdum videmus omnia subjecta ei]], as to the exercise and full manifestation; which will nevertheless come to pass on the last day, when, according to the oracle of Isaias, [[Is 45:25|they shall come to him, and all that resist him shall be confounded|Ad eum venient, et confundentur omnes qui repugnant ei]]. For now many resist Christ and feel no punishment; they blaspheme or dishonour him and suffer no penalty. But after the day of judgement it will not be so. For from then on those who now freely resist him, living impiously, will be subject to him perforce, paying the penalty. Therefore it was fittingly foretold that the world to come is to be subjected to Christ.

paras.t: Eum autem qui modico quam angelis minoratus est, id est, qui in parvo minor factus est angelis, scilicet quantum ad corporis passibilitatem. […] nam, scilicet minoratum, […] passionem mortis, id est merito suæ passionis letalis, mortem sibi inferentis, gloria et honore coronatum: sicut expositum est.
